entries.note: Most likely wishes bad luck so the opposite happens; the hosts reject theatre explanations like being 'in a cast'.

entries.translation: into the wolf's mouth
entries.note: The Italian way of wishing someone good luck, like 'break a leg'.

entries.translation: may the wolf die
entries.note: The set reply to 'in bocca al lupo'; the hosts wonder whether the wolf chokes or dies first.

entries.translation: break your neck and leg
entries.note: The German good-luck wish, very close to the English 'break a leg'.

entries.translation: break your arm and leg
entries.note: The Hungarian good-luck wish, similar to 'break a leg'.

entries.translation: neither fur nor feather
entries.note: Said before a hunt to wish failure, meaning good luck; the reply is 'go to hell'.

entries.term: cost an arm and a leg
entries.note: Means a very heavy price, since losing an arm and a leg would be costly.

entries.term: to cost the eyes of your head
entries.translation: to cost the eyes in your head
entries.note: The French equivalent of 'cost an arm and a leg', where you lose both eyes.

entries.translation: to cost a kidney
entries.note: The Spanish for very expensive; Jess thinks it's the mildest price because you have two kidneys.
Heavy rain; probably from cats and dogs living in roofs being washed into the street.

entries.translation: it's raining ropes/string
entries.note: French for heavy rain, as the drops look like dangling string; Rob's wife once said it in English.

entries.original: il pleut comme vache qui pisse
entries.translation: it's raining like a pissing cow
entries.note: Rob's wife Elodie's suggested French equivalent of 'raining cats and dogs'.

entries.translation: it's raining chair legs
entries.note: The Greek expression for very heavy rain.

entries.translation: axes are falling
entries.note: The Croatian expression for heavy rain, which the hosts find alarming.

entries.translation: it's raining dog poop
entries.note: The Cantonese expression for heavy rain, compared to the French pissing cow.

entries.translation: crowbars are falling
entries.note: The Bosnian expression for heavy rain.

entries.translation: it's raining frogs and platannas
entries.note: Afrikaans for heavy rain; a platanna is a type of frog.

entries.translation: it's raining female trolls
entries.note: The Norwegian expression for heavy rain; the hosts find Scandinavian idioms adorable.

entries.translation: it's snowing kittens
entries.note: A Norwegian weather expression mentioned alongside raining female trolls.
Said of something that will never happen; the hosts look at foreign alternatives.

entries.translation: when hens have teeth
entries.note: French for 'never'; linked to the English 'as rare as hen's teeth'.
Mentioned as a related English idiom used in both Britain and America.

entries.translation: on Saint Glinglin's day
entries.note: Means never, because it names a saint's day that doesn't exist, like 'the 12th of never'.

entries.term: when the crayfish whistles on the mountain
entries.translation: when the crayfish whistles on the mountain
entries.note: A Russian idiom for something that will never happen.

entries.term: slide in on a shrimp sandwich
entries.translation: slide in on a shrimp sandwich
entries.note: Means having a charmed or privileged life, like being born with a silver spoon.

entries.term: you've shat in the blue cupboard
entries.translation: you've [shat] in the blue cupboard
entries.note: Means making a blunder; blue cupboards were valuable once Berlin blue paint arrived in the 1800s.

entries.translation: to tread in the spinach
entries.note: Danish for putting your foot in it; the hosts don't know why spinach is involved.

entries.term: to step on the same rake
entries.translation: to step on the same rake
entries.note: Russian for making an avoidable mistake again, like a cartoon character hit by a rake.

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the crab
entries.translation: thinking about the immortality of the crab
entries.note: Mexican Spanish for daydreaming or being mentally far away.

entries.translation: thinking about blue almonds
entries.note: Polish for daydreaming; the hosts guess a blue almond is doubly pointless.

entries.translation: blowing balloons
entries.note: Colombian Spanish for daydreaming.

entries.translation: thinking about rooster eggs
entries.note: Colombian Spanish for daydreaming; a double entendre on eggs and rooster testicles.

entries.translation: thinking about pregnant birds
entries.note: Venezuelan Spanish for daydreaming.

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the maybug
entries.translation: thinking about the immortality of the maybug
entries.note: Used in Czech or Slovak for daydreaming.

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the mosquito
entries.translation: thinking about the immortality of the mosquito
entries.note: Peruvian Spanish for daydreaming.

entries.translation: to fly around / walk in / live in the clouds
entries.note: Latvian cloud phrases for daydreaming, similar to having your head in the clouds.

entries.term: lie back and think of England
entries.note: A British phrase for letting your mind wander during sex, implying bad sex being endured.

entries.term: the cat climbed onto the roof
entries.translation: the cat climbed onto the roof
entries.note: Means a person or plan seems doomed; it comes from a joke about breaking bad news gradually.

entries.term: to end up like Zabłocki with his soap
entries.translation: to end up like Zabłocki did with his soap
entries.note: For a clever profit scheme that loses money; Zabłocki smuggled soap underwater and it dissolved.

entries.term: not my circus, not my monkeys
entries.translation: not my circus, not my monkeys
entries.note: Disclaims responsibility; Jess thinks English may have borrowed it from Polish.

entries.translation: four cats
entries.note: Means hardly anyone showed up, like 'one man and his dog'.

entries.translation: library rat
entries.note: The Spanish equivalent of 'bookworm'.
Jess explains real bookworms are silverfish, book lice or beetle larvae that eat through old books.

entries.term: better a bird in the hand than a hundred flying
entries.original: más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando
entries.translation: better a bird in the hand than a hundred flying
entries.note: A Spanish variant of 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush'.

entries.term: a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current
entries.translation: a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current
entries.note: Similar to 'you snooze, you lose'.

entries.translation: to pay the duck
entries.note: Brazilian (and Spanish) for being stuck with the bill or made the scapegoat; the hosts can't explain the duck.

entries.translation: lead a cat to water
entries.note: A Spanish version of 'lead a horse to water', harder because it's a cat.

entries.term: raise crows and they will peck out your eyes
entries.translation: raise crows and they will peck out your eyes
entries.note: Bad parenting or bad choices come back to haunt you, like 'you reap what you sow'.
Jess's crow is named after a witch from Terry Pratchett's Discworld.

entries.term: flies don't enter a closed mouth
entries.translation: flies don't enter a closed mouth
entries.note: Keep your mouth shut to stay out of trouble.

entries.translation: to mount a chicken
entries.note: Used when someone makes a loud scene or big fuss, maybe like a mounted chicken would.
Probably from Ecclesiastes, where a bird of the air carries your voice; many European languages share it.

entries.translation: my little finger told me
entries.note: The French equivalent of 'a little bird told me', said while raising the little finger.

entries.term: a magpie brought it on its tail
entries.translation: a magpie brought it on its tail
entries.note: The Russian equivalent of 'a little bird told me', using a magpie.

entries.term: birds hear words spoken by day and mice hear words spoken by night
entries.translation: birds hear words spoken by day and mice hear words spoken by night
entries.note: If the birds don't tell, the mice will; someone always overhears.

entries.term: you do not sue the devil when the court is in hell
entries.translation: you do not sue the devil when the court is in hell
entries.note: A Cornish saying about when authority should solve a problem; Cornish is a revived Celtic language.
Jess gives the native name for the Cornish language (heard as 'Kernow').
Short for 'speak of the devil and he will appear'; many languages have variants.

entries.term: when you talk of the devil, he's not far away
entries.original: Wenn man vom Teufel spricht, ist er nicht weit
entries.translation: when you talk of the devil, he's not far away
entries.note: The German version of 'speak of the devil'.

entries.term: when you speak of the wolf, you see his tail
entries.original: quand on parle du loup, on en voit la queue
entries.translation: when you speak of the wolf, you see his tail
entries.note: The French 'speak of the devil' uses a wolf, reflecting an ancestral European fear of wolves.

entries.term: mention a wolf and the wolf is there
entries.translation: mention a wolf and the wolf is there
entries.note: A Lithuanian equivalent of 'speak of the devil', sent in by a viewer.

entries.translation: between a dog and a wolf
entries.note: Means twilight, when fading light makes it hard to tell a dog from a wolf.
Explained as 'between lights'; the 'twi-' part is related to 'two' and 'between'.

entries.term: the devil knows more because he is old than because he is the devil
entries.original: más sabe el diablo por viejo que por diablo
entries.translation: the devil knows more because he is old than because he is the devil
entries.note: Experience teaches more than talent.

entries.term: to feel it while wearing clogs
entries.translation: to feel it while wearing clogs
entries.note: Something so obvious you could feel it through wooden shoes; the hosts call it very Dutch.

entries.term: all the Moomins are not in the valley
entries.translation: all the Moomins are not in the valley
entries.note: Like 'the lights are on but no one's home'; it refers to the Finnish Moomin books.

entries.term: to lift the cat onto the table
entries.translation: to lift the cat onto the table
entries.note: Raising an awkward subject everyone avoids, like addressing the elephant in the room.
A British political term for raising a shocking issue to distract from another topic.

entries.term: Norwegians are born with skis on their feet
entries.original: nordmenn er født med ski på beina
entries.translation: Norwegians are born with skis on their legs/feet
entries.note: Presented as a typically Norwegian saying about their skiing culture.

entries.term: out on a trip, never sour
entries.translation: out on a trip, never sour
entries.note: A Norwegian saying that going outdoors lifts your mood, like 'go touch grass'.

entries.translation: to walk around the porridge
entries.note: Circling a subject instead of saying what you mean, like beating around the bush.
From hunting: beating bushes to flush out birds instead of going straight for them.

entries.translation: to be parsley in everything
entries.note: For someone who inserts themselves into every conversation or problem, uninvited.

entries.term: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket
entries.translation: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket
entries.note: Describes a stingy person; reaching into the pocket would be painful.

entries.term: broken Irish is better than clever English
entries.translation: broken Irish is better than clever English
entries.note: Encourages people to speak Irish even badly; it rhymes in Irish and carries historical baggage.

entries.translation: hunger is a good sauce
entries.note: Hunger makes food taste better; Jess notes a historical undertone.

entries.term: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge
entries.translation: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge
entries.note: Stay out of other people's business.

entries.term: one's head is a green pepper
entries.translation: one's head is a green pepper
entries.note: Means empty-headed, like a hollow green pepper with a few seeds rattling around.

entries.translation: goldfish poop
entries.note: For someone who trails after another person, like poop dangling from a goldfish.

entries.term: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikkō
entries.original: Nikkō wo minai uchi wa kekkō to iu na
entries.translation: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikkō
entries.note: Praises Nikkō's shrine complex, with a pun between 'Nikkō' and 'kekkō' (splendid).
Attributed by the hosts to Goethe; Naples is so beautiful you could die afterwards.

entries.translation: even monkeys fall from trees
entries.note: Even experts sometimes make mistakes.

entries.term: to have one's tongue in one's pocket
entries.original: avoir la langue dans sa poche
entries.translation: to have one's tongue in one's pocket
entries.note: Quebec French for someone shy or silent.
Compared with the Quebec idiom; Jess finds it a derogatory taunt at someone not speaking.

entries.translation: to hammer nails
entries.note: Quebec French for repeatedly nodding off to sleep.

entries.translation: fasten your toque
entries.note: Quebec French for 'brace yourself'; a toque here is a winter hat, sometimes a chef's hat.

entries.translation: under a frog's ass
entries.note: For a very bad situation, mood or quality, since a frog's bottom is already very low.

entries.term: one is a dog, the other is a hound
entries.translation: one is a dog, the other is a hound
entries.note: Uses two Hungarian words for dog; means six of one, half a dozen of the other.
